opening.headline: We solve the problem of stopping the use of the assistant due to the burden of uploading data every week by comparing the operating burden of upload and connector.
body: The Weekly Reporting Assistant must upload a new reporting file every Monday to be accurate. I uploaded well for the first month, but missed one during a busy week. The missing week's questions were answered with last week's numbers, which eroded trust and ultimately led to team members not using assistants.

In this lesson, we compare the two methods, upload and connector connection, in terms of operational burden. Compare the monthly work of uploading, where people bring in data, with the monthly work of connectors, which open the way to read the app, on a timetable, and see how the operating entity and permission inheritance differ. At the end, we break down the process of deciding whether to change the weekly reporting data to a connector.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the operational burden of uploads and connector connections
You can choose a method based on volume and update frequency.
You can determine the operational burden of the selected method

screens.title: I stopped using it because uploading data every week was a burden.
screens.lead: First, let's look at how the Weekly Reporting Assistant came to a halt. Pay attention to where the first cracks appear.

visual.alt: A weekly calendar with more blank spaces as the schedule for uploading data piles up every Monday.
labels: It stops when a person rests.

paragraphs: The Weekly Reporting Assistant must upload a new reporting file every Monday for it to respond accurately. The person in charge did well for the first month. Then I missed one during a busy week.

The missing week's questions were answered with last week's numbers, and the team members found it difficult to trust the assistant's answers. As trust decreased, use decreased, and eventually team members stopped using the assistant.
The question for this class is this. Which has lower operational burden: upload or connector?

screens.outro: First, let’s think about your data management experience.

screens.title: Who is responsible for uploading repeated material every week?
screens.lead: When you select each representative's card, the instructor's thoughts are revealed. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think first before clicking.

items.prompt: Who updates the data uploaded to the Assistant and when?
items.answer: It is best if there is a designated responsibility and timing. Most of them are posted as soon as I remember who created them. In this case, the person in charge relies on the person's memory, so it becomes the first task to be missed on a busy day.

items.prompt: Is there someone who can post on behalf of the person in charge when he/she is on vacation?
items.answer: If not, the assistant from that period answers with outdated material. Uploading is a representative example of how people stop when they take a break. The person who will act on your behalf and the process must be documented.

items.prompt: What happens to work for which no operator is determined over time?
items.answer: It goes well at first, but it gradually declines, and at some point it becomes a task that no one does. This is why it is said that keeping an assistant in continuous use is more difficult than creating it. It is important to choose a method with low operational burden.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's start by looking at uploads where people submit data.

screens.title: Upload: How people put it
screens.lead: Click the Next Step button to follow the week's uploads in order. Pay attention to who each task belongs to.

visual.alt: Illustration showing the upload process, where a person moves a file into a drawer.

steps.title: What is upload?
steps.body: Uploading is a method where a person directly uploads a file and places it into a project or GPT knowledge. It is the easiest to get started with because the principle is simple and no separate connections are required. However, even if the original changes after uploading, the copy remains the same.

steps.title: 1. Receive the file
steps.body: On Monday morning, your representative receives your new weekly reporting file. The first task is to request the file from the person who has the original or download it directly. This step will already take time if you don't know where the original is.

steps.title: 2. Raise it
steps.body: Upload the received file to the project. The ChatGPT project lets you decide whether to add a file with the same name as Upload anyway or skip it as Skip. You can avoid this check by naming your files differently each week, but old files will pile up.

steps.title: 3. Delete old files
steps.body: In ChatGPT projects, you can open, preview, and delete files from the source list. If you don't delete the old file, last week's numbers will remain and be mixed into the response. When you delete a file from a shared project, it disappears from everyone.

steps.title: 4. Check for omissions
steps.body: Check whether this week's files have been uploaded or old files have been deleted by asking key questions. In a shared project, the owner can add files, and members with editing permissions can also upload or delete files, so you need to check who uploaded them.

steps.title: Operational operations of uploads
steps.body: In summary, there are three operational tasks for upload: updating, deleting old files, and checking for missing files. These three things must be done by a person every week, and if they are missed once, the trustworthiness of the response is shaken.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the upload in action, let's take a look at the connector that opens the way to our app.

screens.title: Connector connections: How to leave the way for apps to be read
screens.lead: Select each tab to see the steps for connecting apps for each product. Once you connect, notice how things change afterward.

visual.alt: A diagram showing apps such as Assistant on the left and Drive and Slack on the right connected by a connecting line with an approval sign.

tabs.label: What is a connector?
tabs.body: Connectors are connections that allow your assistant to get data from your apps and services and, if necessary, take action on them. Rather than moving files to a copy, you are opening a path to where the original is. So, there is no need for people to re-upload the original every time it changes.

tabs.label: ChatGPT
tabs.body: ChatGPT finds and connects to the app in Plugins in Settings. If necessary, select Install plugin to begin setup. After connecting, specify the app with @ in the conversation or select it from the + menu. Apps can request permission before reading or performing operations, preventing unintended reads or writes. Your workspace administrator may change app access.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: Claude browses the Connectors directory in Customize, selects the connector he wants, and clicks Connect or Install to begin setup. Follow the authentication instructions to allow access and you will be connected. In Team and Enterprise plans, the owner must first activate the connector, and even if activated, each member must authenticate before they can use it.

tabs.label: What changes after connection
tabs.body: Once connected, your weekly updates, deletion of old files, and checking for missing files will disappear. Instead, we'll occasionally check your connection status and reach. Operational tasks shift from repetitive human tasks to one-time setup and occasional inspection.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen how both methods work, let's compare how their operating entities and permissions differ.

screens.title: Operating entity and authority inheritance
screens.lead: Use a switch to go back and forth between uploads and connectors to compare who is responsible for what and with whose authority the same data is read.

visual.alt: A side-by-side illustration of a who does it table and authority flow arrows.
labels: Person in charge of continuing to upload
Anyone who has access to the project
Only visible to the extent of my authority

states.label: upload
states.body: The person responsible for operating the upload is the person in charge of continuing the upload. If the person in charge stops updating, the data also stops. In a shared project, the owner can add files, and members with editing permissions can also upload or delete files, so you need to decide who has ultimate responsibility. In terms of permissions, files uploaded to a project are shared by anyone who has access to the project. Please note that even if access is restricted in the original folder, the moment you upload a file, it will be visible to everyone who enters the project.

states.label: connector
states.body: The operator of the connector is the person who first connected and the administrator. The Claude connector inherits each user's permissions from the connected service, preventing access to files or channels that cannot be viewed originally. However, custom connectors that use shared credentials have access only to the extent of those credentials. In Team and Enterprise, owners can add connectors, members can authenticate themselves, and administrators can limit what actions are allowed, such as read-only, on a per-service basis. Administrators can also change app access in the ChatGPT workspace.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the differences in operating entities, let's compare the work for one month with a timetable.

screens.title: Commentary: Comparison of monthly operational tasks of both methods in timetable
screens.lead: As you select each week, you'll see what uploads and connectors need to do that week. Try pressing while thinking about which side is most likely to miss.

items.prompt: Week 1: What do you do on Monday?
items.answer: Upload receives and uploads new reporting files, deletes old files, and verifies that they are uploaded. All three tasks are performed by human hands. The key for connectors is to check connection status and permission scope once at the beginning of the month, and that only needs to be done this week.

items.prompt: Weeks 2 and 3: What about a typical week?
items.answer: Uploading repeats the same three operations. You get used to having the same schedule every week, but it can easily get pushed aside on busy days. The connector has no additional work to do this week. As new reports appear in the original folder, your assistant will read them.

items.prompt: What are the weeks when the person in charge is on vacation?
items.answer: Uploads stop when people take a break, so that week's questions show last week's numbers. The connector follows when the original changes, even if the person takes a break. This difference is the biggest factor in dividing the operating burden between the two methods.

items.prompt: Is there any strain on the connector at all?
items.answer: There is. Because the connector's access range must be accurately determined initially, consultation with the administrator is required when setting it up. It remains to regularly check connection status and permission scope. This doesn't mean the burden is gone, but it moves from repetitive tasks to one-time setup and occasional checks.

items.prompt: How does the month as a whole compare?
items.answer: Four weekly uploads and four deleting old files and checking for omissions fill the calendar. Connectors are mainly inspected at the beginning of each month. The total number of operations varies, but more importantly, points of failure occur weekly for uploads and cluster in settings and permissions for connectors.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the difference with the timetable, let's explain the process of deciding whether to change it to an actual case.

screens.title: Commentary: Decision process for converting weekly reporting data upload to connector
screens.lead: Press the Next Step button to follow the case as the answers move closer to conclusion as questions open one by one.

steps.title: Question 1: Quantity
steps.body: Weekly reporting is not a large file. But there are new files every week. The upload itself is easy because the file size is small, but as the files continue to pile up, repeated updating and organizing becomes a problem.

steps.title: Question 2: Update Frequency
steps.body: The renewal frequency is high, once a week. The upload burden continues, and if the person in charge leaves even once, old data is used. The fact that the renewal frequency is high is the first reason to lean towards connection.

steps.title: Question 3: Source location
steps.body: Reports are in Drive, and there's a Drive connector. Since the source is in a reachable location, the connection is actually possible. If the original was somewhere unreachable, you will need to continue uploading from this question.

steps.title: Question 4: Permissions
steps.body: Team members should only read reports within their scope of authority. The connector fits this need because it honors each user's service permissions. On the other hand, uploading requires you to be more careful in terms of permissions, as the file may be visible to anyone who has access to the project.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: Since the answers to all four questions point to a connection, let's change it to a Drive connection. The instructions state that reporting questions should be answered by looking in the linked reporting folder, and if you can't find them, say they aren't there. After making the change, all that remains is to check your connection status and permission scope at the beginning of the month.

screens.outro: Now that we have reviewed the judgment process, let us summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Summarizes the contents of this class. As you read, answer the initial question: Which has lower operational overhead: uploads or connectors?

paragraphs: The initial question was whether upload or connector would have lower operational burden. The answer depends on the nature of the material, but for frequently updated materials the burden on the connector is low. Uploads require a person to update every week, delete old files, check for omissions, and stop when the person takes a break. Once connected, the connector follows when the source changes, and all that remains is to occasionally check the connection status and access range.

Authority is also an important criterion. Claude Connector honors each user's permissions on connected services, ChatGPT can also request permission before apps can read or act on it, and administrators can adjust access. Uploaded files are shared by those who have access to the project, so the original access restrictions may not be maintained.
The order of choice for a method is volume, update frequency, source location, and permissions. We consider these four things in turn and decide whether to continue uploading or change to connecting.

The reason the weekly reporting assistant stopped in the first scene was operational, not technical. Long-lived assistants are built on low operational overhead. This standard applies equally to all tools: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: The cost of continuing to use the assistant is greater than the cost of creating it. When choosing one, look at how much work it will require you to do each month rather than how easy it is to set up the first time.

glossary.def: This is a method where a person uploads a file directly and puts it into knowledge. It's easy to start, but people have to take care of updating and organizing.
This is a method of connecting the assistant to retrieve data directly from apps and services.
This person is responsible for updating data and checking connection status.
This property follows each user's existing access rights in the service to which the connector is connected.

misconceptions.myth: Once you set up the connector, there is no need for management.
misconceptions.fact: You should regularly check your connection status and reach. Repetitive tasks are reduced, but management does not disappear.
Although it starts out simple, materials that require repeated updating become more burdensome over time.

misconceptions.myth: When you connect the connector, all data is visible.
misconceptions.fact: Only the user's service permissions are visible. You cannot access files or channels that are not originally viewable.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Methods with low operating burden are used for a long time.
Uploads are operated by people and connectors are operated by connections.
The connector follows the user's permissions.
The method is determined by volume, update frequency, source location, and authority.
